name: Tana
tagline: Supertag-based outliner that turns notes into structured knowledge

pricing.notes: Working normalization from the official public pricing structure. Recheck the source page immediately before publication.

tiers.notes: Early-bird price shown on the live page.

tiers.name: Max

tiers.notes: Early-bird price shown on the live page.

pricing.freeTierCaps: 5 hosted meetings/month; 1 connected calendar; 50 AI queries
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual for Pro and Max; annual agreement for Business; 30-day no-card trial of paid features
pricing.hiddenCosts: AI top-ups can be purchased; plans are per user; the displayed Pro and Max prices are explicitly early-bird rates

verdictSummary: The visible structured networked notes loop is buildable, but a credible replacement needs more than the first screen. Tana earns its keep through polish, sync, importers, so expect a weekend or multi-day build and a narrower personal scope.
coreLoopDIY: Build a local-first structured networked notes app with fast capture, full-text search, backlinks, tags, and Markdown export.
replacementScope: narrow personal or very small-team substitute
whyPeopleStillPay: Tana: People pay for a writing surface they trust for years, plus migration tools, sync, and tiny interaction details that disappear into habit.
ongoingBurden: Own schema migrations, backups, sync conflicts, export compatibility, and long-term file readability.

priorArt.name: AppFlowy
priorArt.desc: Local-first open-source workspace with documents and databases.

priorArt.name: Logseq
priorArt.desc: Open-source local knowledge graph and outliner.

alternatives.name: Logseq
alternatives.desc: An outliner with properties, templates and queries; supertags arrive as several smaller ideas.

facts.install: Desktop or mobile installer from the official downloads/releases
facts.dataFormat: The established file-based edition stores pages as Markdown or Org files plus assets in a local graph folder; the newer database-backed edition uses a different local database model
facts.gapVsPaid: Logseq has properties, templates, and queries but no single supertag system that instantly turns blocks into typed records with live structured views like Tana.
facts.setupBlocker: The first decision is whether to stay on the mature file-based edition or adopt the newer database edition and its migration path; either way, sync and backups need deliberate setup

alternatives.name: SiYuan
alternatives.desc: Structured blocks, attributes and database views, with less magic and more switches.

facts.install: Desktop/mobile package, or Docker image for browser-based self-hosting
facts.engines: Built-in AI features connect to OpenAI-compatible APIs using a configured endpoint and key
facts.dataFormat: A workspace stores block documents as structured .sy JSON files plus assets on disk; SQLite files hold indexes and auxiliary state; documents can export to Markdown, HTML, PDF, and Word
facts.gapVsPaid: SiYuan can structure blocks and show database views, but it lacks Tana's fast command-driven supertags and fluid live-search-node workflow.
facts.setupBlocker: The desktop app installs cleanly, but free cross-device sync is not a turnkey feature: official cloud sync is a paid membership feature and Docker hosting does not transparently become desktop/mobile sync

alternatives.name: Trilium Notes
alternatives.desc: Templates, relations and attributes turn notes into records, though the outline is a tree.

facts.install: Desktop release package, or Docker Compose/image for a server and browser client
facts.dataFormat: Notes, hierarchy, attributes, revisions, and most attachments live in a local or server-side SQLite database named document.db; notes can be exported to HTML, Markdown, or OPML
facts.gapVsPaid: Trilium's one-primary-parent tree is much more rigid than Tana's block outliner and supertag-driven views for reusing the same structured information.
facts.setupBlocker: The desktop app is straightforward, but cross-device sync and browser access require operating a Trilium server, persisting document.db, and handling backups and upgrades

notes: Useful boundary case: the first 60 percent of Tana is approachable, but operating the last 40 percent is the real subscription.
prompt:
Build a deliberately narrow personal substitute for Tana, not a full clone.
Use exactly this stack: Tauri 2 + React + TypeScript + SQLite.
Primary job: Build a local-first structured networked notes app with fast capture, full-text search, backlinks, tags, and Markdown export.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: native mobile clients; conflict-safe multi-device sync; mature importers and exporters.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
